newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico City fuel blast injures at least 11.
newsitem.headline: Mexico City fuel blast injures at least 11.

text.p: A towering column of flame lit up Mexico City's night sky on Monday after a giant fuel storage tank owned by state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) exploded hours earlier in this city suburb, injuring at least 11.
Flames lept hundreds of meters (yards) into the air after the initial blast on Monday afternoon quickly spread to a second storage tank, adding to the immense inferno.

Hundreds of exhausted firefighters battled the fire, blamed by officials on a leaky valve, and sprayed cold water and fire-retardant chemicals on other tanks nearby in an effort to prevent them from igniting as well.

Pemex officials said the blaze, although still huge, was under control by late on Monday and would die out after some 105,000 barrels of gasoline stored in the two tanks burned out. They said firefighters were using 8,000 gallons (30,000 liters) of water per second to control the fireball.

A man claiming to be a Mexican Red Cross official told local radio four people had died and more than 900 had suffered smoke inhalation, but Red Cross officials contacted by Reuters said they did not know who he was. Pemex officials said no one died in the accident.

Army troops and state police evacuated up to 1,000 people from the area and sympathetic Mexico City residents called local television and radio stations to offer shelter to those forced from their homes. Schools within 1.4 miles (two km) of the storage facility were cancelled for Tuesday.
An unknown number of residents were treated for smoke inhalation and many complained of a burning sensation in their eyes, witnesses said.
"We heard a loud noise, we didn't know what it was. Then we saw the fire," said a shaken Lourdes Rivas Mendoza, a 30-year-old housewife who lives near the site of the blast.
As the thick, black smoke continued to pour into the air, Mexico City health officials urged residents of this already polluted city to avoid outdoor exercise and stay indoors.

Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo said during a visit to Chile on Monday for a summit of regional leaders that he was following news of the blaze closely and ordered federal emergency aid to the area.

For residents like Rivas, the blast recalled another nightmare nearly 12 years ago, when natural gas tanks in the neighborhood exploded, killing at least 511 people and injuring thousands. The anniversary of that tragedy is just a week away.
TV Azteca television network said local residents had been pressing for some time for the depot to be relocated because of safety concerns.
Monday's explosion occurred at 3:05 p.m. (2105 GMT) at Pemex's storage and distribution center in this industrial suburb, some 11 miles (16 km) from downtown.

Doctors in area hospitals said most victims suffered second- and third-degree burns. Bloodied firemen were seen being taken on stretchers to hospitals, their faces raw with burns and swathed in bandages.

The explosion was the second in recent months at a Pemex installation. On July 26 a blast caused by human error at the firm's Cactus gas processing center in the southern state of Chiapas killed six workers.
In April 1992, an explosion in Mexico's second-biggest city, Guadalajara, killed more than 200 people after gasoline leaked from a Pemex pipeline into the sewer system.
